pedagogy.summary: Mentally adding or subtracting tens to a three-digit number extends the ones-anchor idea one column up: only the tens digit changes, UNLESS the calculation bridges a hundred (then the hundreds digit changes too). Children reuse decade facts (7 tens ± some tens) while keeping the hundreds and ones fixed. It builds directly on finding 10 more/less and on three-digit place value, taught with a place-value chart and a hundred-marked number line.
bestPractices: Anchor the hundreds and ones; operate only on the tens — 345+40 keeps '3_5' and works 40+40 in the tens
Reuse decade bonds and the make-ten idea at the scale of tens for bridging a hundred (372+40 = 372+28+12... via 380/400)
Contrast a non-bridging case (345+40) with a bridging case (372+40) so the child sees when the hundreds digit moves
Build from '10 or 100 more/less' — adding 40 is four steps of ten
Ask the child to predict which digits change before calculating (DfE evidence)
keyRepresentations: Place-value / Gattegno chart (tens row moves; bridging cascades to hundreds)
Number line marked in tens, around the nearest hundred
Base-ten blocks (add/remove ten-rods, exchange at the hundred)
commonMisconceptions: Changing the ones digit instead of the tens (345+40 given as 349)
Failing to bridge a hundred: 372+40 given as 3(11)2 or keeping the tens at 11
Smaller-from-larger in the tens when subtracting bridges down (a hundred not decomposed)
Believing 'only the tens digit ever changes', so bridging-a-hundred cases are mishandled

learn.summary: Mentally adding or subtracting multiples of ten to a three-digit number extends the '10 more/less' idea one column up: usually only the tens digit changes, UNLESS the calculation bridges a hundred, in which case the hundreds digit also changes. Children anchor the hundreds and ones, reuse decade facts in the tens (e.g. 7 tens ± some tens), and use make-ten at the scale of tens when crossing a hundred. Teach with a place-value chart and a number line marked in tens around the nearest hundred, deliberately contrasting non-bridging and bridging cases so the exception is visible.

activities.title: Contrast a non-bridging and a bridging case on a place-value chart
feedback: If the child gives 349 for 345 + 40, they treated 40 as 4 and changed the ones. Re-anchor with the chart: 40 is four tens, so it joins the tens; connect it to '10 more' done four times.

If the child leaves eleven tens for 372 + 40 (writing 3(11)2 / 3112) or keeps the hundreds unchanged, show on the tens number line that the jump crosses 400; use make-ten at the scale of tens (add 28 to reach 400, then 12), or exchange ten ten-rods for one hundred with base-ten blocks.
Reinforce correct predictions by asking the child to name the moment the hundreds digit changes and why.
activities.rationale: Year 3 pupils are expected to add and subtract a three-digit number and tens mentally. Bridging a hundred reuses the make-ten strategy at a larger scale, built on finding 10/100 more or less and on unitising tens, so an explicit non-bridging vs bridging contrast isolates when the hundreds digit moves.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils add and subtract mentally a three-digit number and tens.
Bridging a multiple of ten (here a hundred) reuses the make-ten strategy at a larger scale, built on finding 10/100 more or less and on unitising tens.
learnerActions: Start with 345 on a place-value chart and add 40 mentally: before calculating, predict which digits will change and which will stay the same.
Confirm that only the tens change (4 tens + 4 tens = 8 tens), giving 385, with the hundreds (3) and ones (5) unchanged.
Now try 372 + 40, again predicting first: notice the tens reach eleven, so a hundred is composed and the hundreds digit ticks up — resolve to 412 (reach 400 by adding 28, then add the remaining 12).
Say aloud how 372 + 40 is like 7 tens + 4 tens = 11 tens, and point to where the extra hundred comes from.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding or subtracting tens changes only the tens digit UNLESS the running total of tens crosses a hundred, in which case a hundred is composed (or decomposed) and the hundreds digit changes too — the same kind of exception children already met when crossing a ten.

activities.title: Bridge a hundred downwards when subtracting
feedback: If the child keeps the hundreds at 4 for 431 − 50, show on the tens number line that the jump must cross below 400, and decompose a hundred into ten tens with blocks.
If the child does 5 − 3 in the tens (smaller-from-larger, giving 421), check by adding back: 421 + 50 = 471, not 431, and 421 is only 10 less than 431. Then redo by crossing 400.
Confirm 381 and ask the child to explain where the hundred was decomposed.
activities.rationale: Subtraction that bridges down is the same unitising/make-ten idea applied in reverse; an amount check (is the answer exactly 50 less, and does adding 50 back return the start?) and a tens number line expose the common 'smaller-from-larger' and 'hundreds don't move' errors.
sourceClaims: Bridging a multiple of ten (here a hundred) reuses the make-ten strategy at a larger scale, built on finding 10/100 more or less and on unitising tens.
learnerActions: Work out 431 − 50 mentally, first predicting whether the hundreds digit will change.
Check the size: subtracting 50 should make the answer exactly 50 less than 431, which takes it below 400. Is your answer below 400, and does adding 50 back give 431?
Use a number line marked in tens to show the jump crosses below 400 (431 − 31 = 400, then − 19 more = 381).
If using base-ten blocks, decompose one hundred into ten tens before removing five tens.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtracting tens can bridge a hundred downwards, decomposing a hundred into ten tens; the hundreds digit then decreases, and the result must be smaller than the start.

activities.title: Predict and sort: will the hundreds digit change?
feedback: If a bridging item is sorted as non-bridging: for addition items add the tens together (e.g. 7 tens + 4 tens = 11 tens, which exceeds nine tens); for subtraction items check whether the tens removed exceed the tens in the number (e.g. 431 has 3 tens but 5 tens are removed), which forces crossing below a hundred.
Use a mixed-item check with a 3(11)2-style wrong answer for 372 + 40 (shown as 3112, or as 312 when the hundred is dropped) to surface the overgeneralisation, then re-explain via composing a hundred.
Praise reasoning that correctly anticipates the hundreds change, not just correct final digits.
activities.rationale: Asking children to predict which digits change before calculating, and contrasting bridging with non-bridging items, targets the specific misconception that the hundreds never move; recognition/sorting here supports reasoning but should follow, not replace, the mental construction work.
learnerActions: For a mixed set of items (e.g. 345 + 40, 372 + 40, 462 − 30, 431 − 50), predict for each whether the hundreds digit will change before calculating.
Sort the items into 'bridges a hundred' and 'does not bridge a hundred'.
Calculate each mentally, then check your sort against the answers (385, 412, 432, 381).
Explain in your own words the rule: only the tens change unless the calculation crosses a hundred.
activities.intendedInsight: Deciding in advance whether a calculation bridges a hundred builds the discriminating judgement that prevents the over-generalisation 'only the tens digit ever changes'.

constraints: Multiple-choice or sort-and-check tasks can rehearse and surface the bridging over-generalisation, but they check reasoning rather than build the mental method; keep them after the child has constructed answers mentally.

A static tap-to-reveal chart can show which digit changes as a reference, but it cannot animate the cascade of composing a hundred; pair it with number-line or blocks work so the bridging move is actually traced.

Base-ten blocks and chart/number-line models are approximations and representations of the quantities, not the mental calculation itself; the objective is reliable mental computation, so fade the supports as the child becomes secure.
The 'only the tens digit changes' heuristic is explicitly conditional: always make the bridging exception part of the rule, in both addition and subtraction directions.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched, and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the worked numbers: 345 + 40 = 385; 372 + 40 = 412 (reach 400 by +28, then +12); 462 − 30 = 432 (non-bridging, only tens change); 431 − 50 = 381 (431 − 31 = 400, then − 19 = 381). These check out and are used as stated.
The original source listed the three-item answer as '385, 412, 381' which is correct; retained.

The original 2d-interactive recommendation described the tens wheel for 345 + 40 spinning '4→8' — the tens digit of 345 is 4 and 4+4=8, giving 385, which is consistent. Preserved as a correct example.

The original best practice 'ask the child to predict which digits change before calculating (DfE evidence)' is retained as pedagogy, but neither verbatim source claim directly supports prediction/sorting as a method, so activity 3 lists no source claim.
Independent review trimmed the curriculum claim from activity 2 as topic-only for that activity's method principle; the make-ten/unitising claim remains as the direct support.

Interactive-media design examples (spinning tens wheel cascading to hundreds, number-line-in-tens toggle, live recolouring of changed digits) are retained as optional illustrations of the mechanism, not as mandatory tooling.

probeDeeper: For 345 + 40, which digits changed and which stayed the same? Why?
For 372 + 40, why did the hundreds digit change when it didn't for 345 + 40?
Is 431 − 50 bigger or smaller than 431? Should it be?
How is 372 + 40 like 7 tens + 4 tens? Where does the extra hundred come from?
assess.correctAnswer: 385, 412, 381. 345+40 changes only the tens (385). 372+40 bridges a hundred: tens go 7→9 then over, +12 in tens = 412 (hundreds digit changes). 431−50 bridges down: 431−31 to 400, then −19 more = 381 (hundreds digit changes).

errorPatterns.pattern: Changes the ones digit instead of the tens — '345 + 40 is 349' (adds 4 to the ones)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor with the chart: 40 is four tens, joining the tens. Connect to '10 more' repeated four times.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The ones digit changes rather than the tens; the child treated 40 as 4

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails to bridge a hundred — '372 + 40' leaves eleven tens (3(11)2 / 3112) or keeps the hundreds unchanged
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show on the tens number line that 372+40 crosses 400; make-ten at the scale of tens (add 28 to reach 400, then 12). Exchange ten tens for a hundred with blocks.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 372+40 the tens total reaches eleven but no hundred is composed; hundreds digit unchanged

errorPatterns.pattern: Subtraction bridging down not handled — '431 − 50' keeps the hundreds at 4 or does smaller-from-larger in the tens
errorPatterns.nextMove: On the tens number line show 431−50 must cross below 400; decompose a hundred into ten tens if using blocks. Sanity-check that subtracting makes it smaller.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 431−50 the hundreds digit doesn't drop, or the tens are done as 5−3

responseLevels.gap: Changes the ones instead of the tens, or leaves eleven tens / fails to move the hundreds; believes only the tens digit ever changes.
responseLevels.full: Answers all three mentally, anchoring hundreds and ones, bridges the hundred in both directions, and explains that only the tens change unless the calculation crosses a hundred.
responseLevels.partial: Handles the non-bridging case and can bridge a hundred with a number line or blocks, but not yet reliably in his head; may miss direction on subtraction.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to do these mentally, thinking aloud: 345 + 40, then 372 + 40, then 431 − 50. After each, ask which digits changed. Watch the two that cross a hundred.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 345+40 confirms the child anchors hundreds and ones and operates on the tens. 372+40 and 431−50 bridge a hundred — a child who thinks only the tens digit ever changes leaves eleven tens or fails to move the hundreds, while a correct child cascades to the hundreds. The non-bridging vs bridging contrast isolates the error.
